name: Weleda Skin Food

card.summary: A rich plant-oil and wax cream from Weleda used on dry skin to soften and add glow.
card.note: Rich balms can feel heavy on oily or acne-prone skin.

quick.overview:
Skin Food is a thick, botanical moisturiser from the Swiss company Weleda, which makes natural cosmetics on anthroposophic principles. It is a cult product used on dry patches, hands, elbows and as a face and makeup-prep cream.

The appearance payoff is smoother, softer, more luminous-looking skin. Emollient creams generally work by holding moisture in the skin surface.
quick.how: Typically applied as a rich cream to dry areas, or in a thin layer under makeup for glow. It is an everyday over-the-counter product.
quick.risks: Generally ordinary for a rich cosmetic: heavy textures may not suit oily skin, and plant ingredients can cause reactions in people with allergies. Consult the ingredient label.

lead: Weleda Skin Food is a rich plant-based cream marketed for dry skin. It is a staple of Weleda, a Swiss-headquartered company founded in 1920 by Rudolf Steiner and Ita Wegman and run on anthroposophic principles [1].
People use it to soften rough areas and to give skin a dewy finish. Weleda says it sources botanical ingredients grown with biodynamic methods and emphasises whole-plant formulas [1].
No studies of this product itself were found. Research on emollients generally exists; a large randomised trial of regular emollient use in infants examined atopic dermatitis prevention [2].

chain: Rich oils and waxes occlude the skin surface
angle.text: It is used as a heavy moisturiser to smooth dry skin and add glow. Some users layer it under makeup.

paras: Weleda was formed from companies founded in 1920 and merged in 1922; the Weleda name was registered in 1928 [1]. It is headquartered in Arlesheim, Switzerland, and holds Union for Ethical BioTrade certification (2018) [1]. Wikipedia describes anthroposophic medicine as a pseudoscience; Weleda markets its products as natural cosmetics [1].
Skin Food is part of Weleda's skin care line. Wikipedia does not list its ingredients [1]; users report using it on dry skin, hands and as a pre-makeup base.

No studies found. For emollients in general, the 2020 PreventADALL trial randomised infants to regular skin emollient from two weeks of age to test prevention of atopic dermatitis [2]; it did not test this product.

timeline.event: Steiner and Wegman found the companies that become Weleda [1]
